# Testing AI Scientist v3 with its actual evaluator: 26 circles and scientific evidence

**AI disclosure: ChatGPT authored this article and the candidate code. This is not a manuscript produced by the official automated research pipeline.**

The most valuable component of an automated laboratory may be the evaluator: a way to check an experiment without trusting the agent's own account. We ran the official Circle Packing evaluator shipped with Sakana AI's Agentic Scientist v3 on a CPU. A fixed-center linear programming candidate improved the sum of radii from the official starter's 0.959764 to 2.500000. The evaluator was unchanged, and an independent geometry calculation and replay agreed. This is a comparison against a weak starter, not a record or an evaluation of the complete scientist.

![Actual starter and candidate scores](/assets/research/ac03v3-cover.svg)

## Orchestrate existing coding agents instead of rebuilding them

The [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18933) and [official announcement](https://sakana.ai/agentic-scientist/) describe a system that uses existing coding agents, such as Codex and Claude Code, to conduct scientific investigations. A task description specifies what matters. The six default phases draft the task, investigate ideas, run ablations, conduct a sealed final evaluation, analyze the results, and write the paper. Optional review and revision follow. Run-local artifacts preserve the evidence for later inspection.

![The six phases and our limited execution scope](/assets/research/ac03v3-pipeline.svg)

The official CLI recommends Docker and invokes coding agents through Headless with broad tool permissions. Such agents should not be given unrestricted access to a production host. A separate execution environment needs limited credentials, filesystem access, networking, resource budgets, and process controls. We did not establish an isolated native agent runner or an approved API budget, so no agent was launched.

## The mathematical problem

Place 26 circles inside a unit square and maximize their total radius. Let each center be (x_i,y_i) and its radius r_i. The objective is the sum of the radii. Each radius must be nonnegative and no larger than the minimum distance from its center to the four borders. Each pair of circles must satisfy r_i+r_j ≤ the Euclidean distance between its centers. There are 325 such pairs.

Joint optimization of centers and radii is not a linear problem. With centers fixed, however, all pairwise distances are constants. The objective and constraints in the radii are linear. We chose five rows containing 5, 5, 6, 5, and 5 centers, respectively, and solved the resulting linear program with SciPy's HiGHS solver. We imposed a positive lower bound of 1e-5 and subtracted 1e-9 from each solved radius to preserve numerical slack. This is a solution for one fixed arrangement, not a global optimum across all center positions.

## Actual execution

We pinned the official repository to revision f8ae47d324edcb6c0d430552f1c7729748c0d411, downloaded its evaluator, capture utility and starter, and recorded SHA-256 hashes. The unchanged official evaluator CLI ran three times: starter, candidate, and candidate replay. Our available NumPy 2.4.4 and SciPy 1.18.0 differ from the pinned requirements 2.4.2 and 1.17.1. Thus the evaluator is native but the environment is not an exact reproduction.

![The actual evaluated circle arrangements](/assets/research/ac03v3-packing.svg)

| Measure | Official starter | Candidate |
|---|---:|---:|
| Sum of radii | 0.959764217 | 2.499999974 |
| Minimum radius | 0 | 0.083333332 |
| Official correctness | true | true |

The improvement relative to the starter is 160.48%. The starter contains zero-radius circles, permitted by the official evaluator. It is a weak comparator, and this percentage should not be interpreted as frontier performance. All 26 candidate radii are positive. Coordinates, radii and scores matched exactly in the replay. A separate Python standard-library geometry calculation verified all 325 pairs, all borders, and the reported sum. The minimum edge slack is approximately 1e-9 and the minimum pair slack approximately 2e-9.

## An evidence gate for Anicca

A candidate score is meaningful only when its constraints hold. Our ManagerBench checker rejects invalid shapes, nonfinite numbers, negative radii, overlapping circles, boundary violations, and incorrect reported sums. Seven unit tests check those conditions against the actual candidate and modified test fixtures. This is an independent implementation of arithmetic, not independent peer review. The public problem has already been observed; this is not a sealed unseen-task evaluation. We did not train Manager or measure any mobile product outcomes.

The full reproduction still needs an isolated six-phase run, exact dependency versions, stronger published baselines, actual time and cost, failed attempts, sealed evaluation and independent review. [Issue #811](https://github.com/Daisuke134/anicca-ops/issues/811) tracks those gates. The practical lesson is to reuse existing research infrastructure and let evidence, rather than the agent's confidence, determine whether a claim is accepted.

Sources: [official pinned code](https://github.com/SakanaAI/AI-Scientist-v3/tree/f8ae47d324edcb6c0d430552f1c7729748c0d411), [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18933).
